note: Every repository is pinned to a commit SHA rather than a branch, so a run today and a run in two years scan the same merges. Re-pinning is a deliberate act: bump `pinnedAt`, update the SHAs, and keep the old results file — a corpus that silently drifts cannot be used to compare two versions of an engine.
selection: v2 — selected on MEASURED merge history, not language coverage: candidates were probed with `git rev-list --merges` plus a merge-tree conflict-rate sample (60 recent merges). Dropped: rust-lang/cargo (zero conflicted merges — merge queue), django/django (10), vuejs/core (35, squash-merge; it was also the 92-95% showcase, which is exactly why keeping it would have been flattering rather than informative). Probed and rejected: kubernetes, rails, godot (0/60 conflicted — merge queues). Every repository is pinned to a commit SHA; re-pinning is a deliberate act recorded in this field. v3 (2026-09-25) — added three repositories, probed with the same method (rev-list --merges over two years, plus merge-tree on the 60 most recent merges): umbraco/Umbraco-CMS 41/60 conflicted, dotnet/efcore 23/60, microsoft/vscode 13/60. The v2 repos keep their pins. Probed and rejected, for too few conflicts (at most 8/60): dotnet/roslyn, jellyfin/jellyfin, dotnet/maui, abpframework/abp, spring-projects/spring-boot, swiftlang/swift, odoo/odoo (forward-ports are cherry-picks), rust-lang/rust (bors: merges are tested before they land), meilisearch/meilisearch. Rejected for having no recent merges: AvaloniaUI/Avalonia (squash), NuGet/NuGet.Client (last merge 2021), rustdesk/rustdesk, servo/servo. The Rust, Java, Swift and Python ecosystems probed leave almost no conflicted merges in their history, so Rust stays covered by tauri alone.

repos.name: prettier/prettier
repos.why: A formatter's own repo: an adversarial case for whitespace_only, since the code is already normalised.

repos.name: gohugoio/hugo
repos.why: Go, with go.mod/go.sum churn — a lockfile format the engine does NOT special-case, kept in deliberately.

repos.name: tauri-apps/tauri
repos.why: Mixed-language monorepo with changesets — the shape GitWand's own users most often have.

repos.name: laravel/framework
repos.why: PHP, very high contributor turnover, many small overlapping edits.

repos.name: expressjs/express
repos.why: Small and old. Included as a control: a repo where the engine should have little to do.

repos.name: symfony/symfony
repos.why: Back-merge culture (5.4 → 6.4 → 7.x) with composer.json conflicts in half the conflicted merges — the divergent-conventions candidate the lot-F gate needs.

repos.name: git/git
repos.why: Integration-branch workflow, conflicts hand-resolved by the maintainers — the highest-quality human-merge ground truth available.

repos.name: twbs/bootstrap
repos.why: Design-system repo: _variables.scss conflicts — a file family none of the format resolvers special-case, kept in as an adversarial case.

repos.name: umbraco/Umbraco-CMS
repos.why: Forward-merge culture (release/N → vN/dev → main): the first real .NET code in the corpus. The conflicted files in the probe were C# (75), TypeScript from the backoffice (73), package.json/package-lock.json (63), version.json (13) and a few .csproj/.props.

repos.name: dotnet/efcore
repos.why: Dependency-flow merges between release branches: its conflicts are almost all version numbers in eng/Version.Details.xml, global.json, Versions.props and NuGet.config, formats the engine does not special-case. Kept as an adversarial case for version-identity conflicts, not as a measure of C# resolution.

repos.name: microsoft/vscode
repos.why: A modern TypeScript codebase whose feature branches merge main back in, where most modern repos squash. 17 of the 25 conflicted files in the probe were .ts.
